subject: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models

messages.author: fba1e33bd69e01a2
messages.subject: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
parts:
Dear all,

My name is Luca Petroni. I am currently working on interspecific spatial interactions among carnivores, but I am encountering fit issues in occupancy models using a "stacked" dataset.

Specifically, my dataset consists of continuous camera-trapping data collected over a year across 50 sites in a mountainous region. I stacked the data by month, resulting in 600 site-months (50 sites × 12 months) with 10 survey occasions (detection/non-detections aggregated by 3 days). I have been fitting the models in JAGS using jagsUI, incorporating a random site effect on species occupancy to account for pseudo-replication, and adding covariates for both occupancy and detection probabilities. Additionally, I used the goodness-of-fit assessment code from AHM2, summarizing the detections by site-month (row). Unfortunately, my results show a severe lack of fit for all the models, regardless of the combinations of covariates used, with Bayesian p-values of 0.

Interestingly, the fit only improves when introducing random site-month effects (i.e., 600 random terms per species) on detection probabilities. Therefore, I tested the fit of single-species models too (in spOccupancy), and the results were the same for all of them: bpv= 0. In this case, however, adding a random site effect on the detection probability was enough to obtain decent fit for most species. However, for the widespread and more abundant ones, only adding the random site-month effect worked out the fit issues.
Referring to MacKenzie and Bailey’s 2004 paper, this severe lack of fit may stem from a higher-than-expected frequency of detection histories with all 1s, which are indeed present for those abundant and widespread species in our study. Since I tested various covariates, unexplained site heterogeneity seems an unlikely cause. Instead, local differences in species density may be a more plausible explanation, particularly for widespread species, also given the stacked structure of my dataset, which includes repeated monthly sampling at the same sites. I even tried to fit the models on daily detection/non-detection data (i.e., 30 survey occasions), to increase the potential variability in the detection histories, but the results were always the same.

I would greatly appreciate your perspective on this issue. Do you think adding a random site-month effect on detection probabilities is justified in this context? Or might there be alternative strategies you’d recommend to address this lack of fit, especially given the size and structure of our dataset?
Thank you all in advance for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Luca Petroni

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
parts:
Hey Luca, 

In my experience, having bad BPVs with these types of models is quite common unless you essentially overfit with adding those random effects. Are you assessing the BPV for each species, or all of them together?

Also, I'm pretty sure we've collectively been doing this PPCs "wrong" with these models. It is typical to condition the posterior predictive distribution on your latent occupancy states, i.e., yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(z[i] * p[i, j]), where i and j reference sites and surveys, respectively. However, this isn't really the posterior predictive distribution. For that, you should do zrep[i] ~ dbern(psi[i]), yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(zrep[i] * p[i, j]), i.e., first simulating new z's and then simulating yreps conditional on them. I don't think it'll make your lack of fit go away, but you could give it a crack. Some of the posterior predictive plotting functionality in the bayesplot is quite useful for visualising the posterior predictive predictive distribution alongside your observed data. I assume your model includes species random effects, btw?

Cheers,

Matt

messages.author: fba1e33bd69e01a2
messages.subject: Re: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
parts:
Dear Matt,

thanks for the answer. I usually calculate the chi-squared discrepancy separately for all the species but sum them to have a measure of the overall model fit. 

I was also thinking about simulating new presence/absence as you suggested, but I tried going single-species with the spOccupancy functions before adding to the JAGS models. Nevertheless, the single-species models fitted in spOccupancy highlighted the same issue, but I did not verify how the discrepancy measures are computed in the ppcOcc( ) function.

As for your last point, the multi-species model includes a random site effect on single-species natural parameters (I have 4 target species, so f1, f2, f3 and f4) but none on the co-occurrence natural parameters (f12, f13, f14, f23, f24, f34, as I only considered pairwise interactions). Then, I have another random site effect on  the detection probabilities for all the species (p1, p2, p3 and p4), but for at least two of them the site-month random is needed, otherwise the overall fit goes to 0.

I do not have random species effects. Should I include them? What is the rationale behind this choice?

Thanks again.

Best,
Luca

messages.author: fba1e33bd69e01a2
messages.subject: Re: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
parts:
Dear Matt,

the model is basically mirroring the multi-species model with interactions from Rota et al. (2016), the same that is implemented in the unmakred package through the occuMulti( ) function. It accounts for interactions among species, therefore their occupancy probabilities are linked and not estimated independently. Specifically, Z is defined as a categorical with x possible values,with x=16 for 4 species: 0000,1000, 0100, 0010, 0001, 1100, 1010, and so on (a multivariate binomial) each with its own probability Psi[x], and natural parameters for single-species occupancy and co-occurrence are expressed as log[Psi[x]/(1-Psi[x])]. 
I have never found random species effects used in this modelling framework, but i could try and see where it will get me.

Moreover, I can tell you another interesting thing supporting my guess about differences in local densities. Adding a simple measure of detection rate (number of detections in a month divided by days the camera was active in the month) as a covariate on detection probability in single-species models always drags the bpv to exactly 1. However, there is no way I can control for such punctual/local differences, especially in a stacked framework. 

Best, 

Luca

messages.subject: Re: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
parts:
Hey Luca,

Nevermind, I wasn't familiar with the model structure. I thought you were just estimating psi and wanted to make sure you were doing so separately for each species. 

Have you considered a different observation model? You could use the observed counts of detections with a Poisson observation model instead of a binary observation model where you essentially collapse those counts to 1s and 0s. I'm not sure to what extent that will help with your model fit, but it should help you hone in on your detection rates a bit better.

Cheers,

Matt

Il giorno martedì 12 novembre 2024 alle 08:39:15 UTC+1 matthijs....@gmail.com ha scritto:
Hey Luca, 

In my experience, having bad BPVs with these types of models is quite common unless you essentially overfit with adding those random effects. Are you assessing the BPV for each species, or all of them together?

Also, I'm pretty sure we've collectively been doing this PPCs "wrong" with these models. It is typical to condition the posterior predictive distribution on your latent occupancy states, i.e., yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(z[i] * p[i, j]), where i and j reference sites and surveys, respectively. However, this isn't really the posterior predictive distribution. For that, you should do zrep[i] ~ dbern(psi[i]), yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(zrep[i] * p[i, j]), i.e., first simulating new z's and then simulating yreps conditional on them. I don't think it'll make your lack of fit go away, but you could give it a crack. Some of the posterior predictive plotting functionality in the bayesplot is quite useful for visualising the posterior predictive predictive distribution alongside your observed data. I assume your model includes species random effects, btw?

Cheers,

Matt

On Tue, Nov 12, 2024 at 6:31 PM Luca Petroni <petroni...@gmail.com> wrote:
Dear all,

My name is Luca Petroni. I am currently working on interspecific spatial interactions among carnivores, but I am encountering fit issues in occupancy models using a "stacked" dataset.

Specifically, my dataset consists of continuous camera-trapping data collected over a year across 50 sites in a mountainous region. I stacked the data by month, resulting in 600 site-months (50 sites × 12 months) with 10 survey occasions (detection/non-detections aggregated by 3 days). I have been fitting the models in JAGS using jagsUI, incorporating a random site effect on species occupancy to account for pseudo-replication, and adding covariates for both occupancy and detection probabilities. Additionally, I used the goodness-of-fit assessment code from AHM2, summarizing the detections by site-month (row). Unfortunately, my results show a severe lack of fit for all the models, regardless of the combinations of covariates used, with Bayesian p-values of 0.

Interestingly, the fit only improves when introducing random site-month effects (i.e., 600 random terms per species) on detection probabilities. Therefore, I tested the fit of single-species models too (in spOccupancy), and the results were the same for all of them: bpv= 0. In this case, however, adding a random site effect on the detection probability was enough to obtain decent fit for most species. However, for the widespread and more abundant ones, only adding the random site-month effect worked out the fit issues.
Referring to MacKenzie and Bailey’s 2004 paper, this severe lack of fit may stem from a higher-than-expected frequency of detection histories with all 1s, which are indeed present for those abundant and widespread species in our study. Since I tested various covariates, unexplained site heterogeneity seems an unlikely cause. Instead, local differences in species density may be a more plausible explanation, particularly for widespread species, also given the stacked structure of my dataset, which includes repeated monthly sampling at the same sites. I even tried to fit the models on daily detection/non-detection data (i.e., 30 survey occasions), to increase the potential variability in the detection histories, but the results were always the same.

I would greatly appreciate your perspective on this issue. Do you think adding a random site-month effect on detection probabilities is justified in this context? Or might there be alternative strategies you’d recommend to address this lack of fit, especially given the size and structure of our dataset?
Thank you all in advance for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Luca Petroni

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: GOF Issues in stacked occupancy models
parts:
Hey,

There's a few things you could do. You could just model the number of detections per species and day (or whatever occasion interval you choose) as Poisson distribution, i.e., y[i, j, m] ~ dpois(lambda[i, j, m]), where you model the site-, survey-, and species-specific detection rates lambda. However, this ignores the non-independence of detections, i.e. with the same animal moving past the device multiple times. Clark Rushing wrote a paper about continuous time CMR where you can account for that with a Hawkes process, which is a self-exciting process that essentially lets prior observations influence the detection rates of next observations (i.e., detection peaks right after an individual is detected becasue it might trigger the camera more than once or it might be a few animals together). For this you have to specify the log-likelihood which I know how to do in Stan, but not in JAGS, but I'm sure someone can help you. I think you need the zeros or ones trick which I never wrapped my head around.

Matt

For this you have to specify the log-likelihood which I know how to do in Stan, but not in JAGS, but I'm sure someone can help you. I think you need the zeros or ones trick which I never wrapped my head around.

Matt

Il giorno martedì 12 novembre 2024 alle 08:39:15 UTC+1 matthijs....@gmail.com ha scritto:
Hey Luca, 

In my experience, having bad BPVs with these types of models is quite common unless you essentially overfit with adding those random effects. Are you assessing the BPV for each species, or all of them together?

Also, I'm pretty sure we've collectively been doing this PPCs "wrong" with these models. It is typical to condition the posterior predictive distribution on your latent occupancy states, i.e., yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(z[i] * p[i, j]), where i and j reference sites and surveys, respectively. However, this isn't really the posterior predictive distribution. For that, you should do zrep[i] ~ dbern(psi[i]), yrep[i, j] ~ dbern(zrep[i] * p[i, j]), i.e., first simulating new z's and then simulating yreps conditional on them. I don't think it'll make your lack of fit go away, but you could give it a crack. Some of the posterior predictive plotting functionality in the bayesplot is quite useful for visualising the posterior predictive predictive distribution alongside your observed data. I assume your model includes species random effects, btw?

Cheers,

Matt

Dear all,

My name is Luca Petroni. I am currently working on interspecific spatial interactions among carnivores, but I am encountering fit issues in occupancy models using a "stacked" dataset.

Specifically, my dataset consists of continuous camera-trapping data collected over a year across 50 sites in a mountainous region. I stacked the data by month, resulting in 600 site-months (50 sites × 12 months) with 10 survey occasions (detection/non-detections aggregated by 3 days). I have been fitting the models in JAGS using jagsUI, incorporating a random site effect on species occupancy to account for pseudo-replication, and adding covariates for both occupancy and detection probabilities. Additionally, I used the goodness-of-fit assessment code from AHM2, summarizing the detections by site-month (row). Unfortunately, my results show a severe lack of fit for all the models, regardless of the combinations of covariates used, with Bayesian p-values of 0.

Interestingly, the fit only improves when introducing random site-month effects (i.e., 600 random terms per species) on detection probabilities. Therefore, I tested the fit of single-species models too (in spOccupancy), and the results were the same for all of them: bpv= 0. In this case, however, adding a random site effect on the detection probability was enough to obtain decent fit for most species. However, for the widespread and more abundant ones, only adding the random site-month effect worked out the fit issues.
Referring to MacKenzie and Bailey’s 2004 paper, this severe lack of fit may stem from a higher-than-expected frequency of detection histories with all 1s, which are indeed present for those abundant and widespread species in our study. Since I tested various covariates, unexplained site heterogeneity seems an unlikely cause. Instead, local differences in species density may be a more plausible explanation, particularly for widespread species, also given the stacked structure of my dataset, which includes repeated monthly sampling at the same sites. I even tried to fit the models on daily detection/non-detection data (i.e., 30 survey occasions), to increase the potential variability in the detection histories, but the results were always the same.

I would greatly appreciate your perspective on this issue. Do you think adding a random site-month effect on detection probabilities is justified in this context? Or might there be alternative strategies you’d recommend to address this lack of fit, especially given the size and structure of our dataset?
Thank you all in advance for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Luca Petroni
